intro_paper.title: The comparisons of data mining techniques for the predictive accuracy of probability of default of credit card clients

business_problem: Predict whether a credit-card holder will default on next month's payment (Oct 2005) using 6 months of repayment status, bill and payment history plus limit and demographics. The bank uses the score to flag high-risk cardholders for intervention (limit reduction, collections outreach). Trade-off: false positives add credit friction for good customers (lost revenue, churn); false negatives are missed defaults (charge-off losses). With a ~22% default rate, accuracy is misleading, so the pipeline optimises F1 and reports ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, precision and recall, then picks an explicit probability cutoff.

target.definition: default payment next month (1 = default, 0 = no default)

PAY_n.9: payment delay for nine months and above

EDUCATION.handling: remap to 4 ('others'): rare and semantically 'not one of the named levels'

PAY_n.interpretation: -2 = inactive cycle (no balance owed, no new charges); 0 = revolving / minimum met (minimum paid on time, balance carried forward)
PAY_n.handling: preserve as distinct ordinal codes; they are behaviourally different from -1 (paid in full) and carry different default risk

definitions.financial_behavior: No balance owed on the previous statement (n+1) and no new charges through month n's closing date (BILL_AMT_n <= 0).
Cleared the entire previous statement (n+1) on or before its due date; any positive BILL_AMT_n reflects new purchases in cycle n.
Paid at least the minimum due on the previous statement (n+1) by its due date, carrying the remaining balance forward with interest.
Number of consecutive due dates without meeting the minimum payment (9 = 9 or more).

rules: Statements run on rolling cycles that start on a date in one month and close on a date in the next; a statement is always named after the month in which it closes.

PAY_n counts consecutive payment due dates where at least the minimum payment due was missed, not billing cycles elapsed since a purchase. Paying at least the minimum by the deadline keeps the account current (PAY_n = 0); the window between a statement's closing date and its due date is a normal grace period (0 cycles late).
billing_cycle.example_cycle: 16th-to-15th cycle, payment due on the 5th of the following month

example.note: A swipe on Aug 14 lands on the August statement (BILL_AMT2).
A swipe on Aug 16 lands on the September statement (BILL_AMT1). On Sep 15 the bank evaluates whether the Sep 5 due date for the August bill was met and records that status in PAY_1.

cash_flow: PAY_AMT1 sums all cash received Sep 1 - Sep 30 (calendar month).
A payment on Sep 4 (before the Sep 15 close) counts in PAY_AMT1 and is deducted from BILL_AMT1.
A payment on Sep 22 (after the close) counts in PAY_AMT1 but is NOT deducted from BILL_AMT1; it carries to October's statement, outside the 6-month window.

delinquency_progression.explanation: BILL_AMT2 newly generated; grace period active, not yet late.
Sep 5 due date missed: 1 deadline passed without the minimum.
Sep 5 and Oct 5 missed: 2 consecutive delinquent due dates.
Sep 5, Oct 5 and Nov 5 missed: 3 consecutive delinquent due dates.

accounting_rules.BILL_AMT_n: Statement balance, a snapshot on month n's statement closing date: previous unpaid balance + new cycle purchases + interest/fees - payments posted on or before the closing date.
accounting_rules.PAY_AMT_n: Cash received within calendar month n (1st to month end); may include payments made before or after month n's closing date, so BILL_AMT_n = BILL_AMT_(n+1) - PAY_AMT_n + new spend does not hold strictly within a single month.
accounting_rules.PAY_n: Repayment status, a snapshot on month n's closing date of how the customer handled the previous statement (n+1) by its due date.

billing_mechanics.empirical_check: The rules above are the project's domain definition. The EDA tests them against the data (artifacts/eda_summary.json -> domain_rule_checks). Two measured deviations: (1) a 'paid in full' status in month k is confirmed by statement k being covered by the following month's payment (PAY_AMT_(k-1) >= BILL_AMT_k) in ~98-99% of rows, versus ~73-80% for the section-4 pairing (PAY_AMT_k >= BILL_AMT_(k+1)), i.e. the data aligns status codes one month later than the rule; (2) '-2 => BILL_AMT_n <= 0' holds for only ~33-71% of -2 rows. Neither affects the engineered features, which use the status sequence and per-month amounts directly. Timing caveat: under the rule PAY_1 holds no October information; under the data's alignment it may partly reflect October payments (an ablation without PAY_1's information costs about 0.04 CV F1).

uci_variable_info:
This research employed a binary variable, default payment (Yes = 1, No = 0), as the response variable. This study reviewed the literature and used the following 23 variables as explanatory variables:
X1: Amount of the given credit (NT dollar): it includes both the individual consumer credit and his/her family (supplementary) credit.
X2: Gender (1 = male; 2 = female).
X3: Education (1 = graduate school; 2 = university; 3 = high school; 4 = others).
X4: Marital status (1 = married; 2 = single; 3 = others).
X5: Age (year).
X6 - X11: History of past payment. We tracked the past monthly payment records (from April to September, 2005) as follows: X6 = the repayment status in September, 2005; X7 = the repayment status in August, 2005; . . .;X11 = the repayment status in April, 2005. The measurement scale for the repayment status is: -1 = pay duly; 1 = payment delay for one month; 2 = payment delay for two months; . . .; 8 = payment delay for eight months; 9 = payment delay for nine months and above.
X12-X17: Amount of bill statement (NT dollar). X12 = amount of bill statement in September, 2005; X13 = amount of bill statement in August, 2005; . . .; X17 = amount of bill statement in April, 2005. 
X18-X23: Amount of previous payment (NT dollar). X18 = amount paid in September, 2005; X19 = amount paid in August, 2005; . . .;X23 = amount paid in April, 2005.

intro_paper.title: The comparisons of data mining techniques for the predictive accuracy of probability of default of credit card clients

additional_info.summary: This research aimed at the case of customers' default payments in Taiwan and compares the predictive accuracy of probability of default among six data mining methods. From the perspective of risk management, the result of predictive accuracy of the estimated probability of default will be more valuable than the binary result of classification - credible or not credible clients. Because the real probability of default is unknown, this study presented the novel Sorting Smoothing Method to estimate the real probability of default. With the real probability of default as the response variable (Y), and the predictive probability of default as the independent variable (X), the simple linear regression result (Y = A + BX) shows that the forecasting model produced by artificial neural network has the highest coefficient of determination; its regression intercept (A) is close to zero, and regression coefficient (B) to one. Therefore, among the six data mining techniques, artificial neural network is the only one that can accurately estimate the real probability of default.
